common_name: Gold Nugget Hens and Chicks (Chartreuse-Gold Sempervivum)

planting.note: Set offsets directly on the surface of gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; firm rosettes in place rather than burying the crown.

directions: Gold Nugget forms neat rosettes of glowing chartreuse-gold foliage that develops coral to salmon tips as nights cool in fall and spring, fading toward greener tones in the heat of summer. Grow in lean, mineral, fast-draining soil in full sun, since strong light is what triggers the brightest color contrast; in shade the rosettes stay flatly green. Water only when the soil has dried, as standing moisture around the crown is the most common cause of rot in any hens and chicks. Like other sempervivums, individual rosettes are monocarpic and die after flowering, but the mother plant continuously produces offsets on short stolons that quickly fill in a rock garden, trough, or wall crevice.

planting.note: Root branch cuttings in fast-draining succulent mix after allowing cut ends to callus for several days; grow in full sun for the deepest purple color.

directions: Atropurpureum is the classic older purple-leaved selection of tree aeonium, forming branching, woody stems topped with rosettes that shift from green in shade to deep wine-purple to nearly maroon-bronze in full sun, a softer and more bronze-toned purple than the near-black Zwartkop selection derived from it. Grow in well-drained, gritty soil in full sun, watering regularly during the cool-season growth period and cutting back sharply during summer dormancy when the plant is more prone to rot. It branches naturally as it ages, and older plants can be kept compact and multiplied by taking stem cuttings, which root readily. Protect from frost, since temperatures much below freezing will damage or kill the exposed stems and rosettes.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in fast-draining succulent mix after callusing; grow in full sun to light afternoon shade for the darkest foliage color.

directions: Voodoo is a compact, freely branching aeonium selection prized for its densely clustered rosettes of glossy, near-black maroon-purple leaves, staying shorter and bushier than larger tree-form purple aeoniums. Grow in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot inland climates, since intense heat combined with strong sun can bleach or scorch the darkest color out of the foliage. Water during the cool-season active growth period and reduce sharply in summer, when the plant rests and is more susceptible to rot from excess moisture. It clusters and offsets readily at the base, making it easy to propagate by dividing rooted offsets or taking stem cuttings, and it makes an effective color contrast planted among gray or green-leaved succulents.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to light shade; established plants self-sow readily in mild-winter gardens.

directions: Aeonium leucoblepharum forms loosely branching clusters of pale olive-green to yellow-green rosettes, each leaf edged with a fine fringe of pale hair-like cilia that gives the species its 'white-lashed' name. Native to the Canary Islands and parts of East Africa, it is one of the more heat-tolerant and easygoing aeoniums, growing readily from cuttings and often self-seeding in favorable mild-climate gardens. Plant in fast-draining, gritty soil in full sun to light shade, watering through the cool growing season and letting the soil dry between waterings in summer dormancy. Clusters of small star-shaped yellow flowers appear on branched stalks above the rosettes in spring, after which flowering rosettes die back but the surrounding clump continues to spread.

planting.note: Pot offsets in a fast-draining succulent mix and grow in bright indirect light or light shade, sheltering from harsh direct midday sun.

directions: Native to the winter-rainfall Northern Cape and Namaqualand region of South Africa, Gasteria pillansii forms low clumping rosettes of thick, tongue-shaped, dark green leaves densely covered in raised silvery-white spots and tubercles. Grow in a fast-draining, gritty succulent mix in bright indirect light or light shade, since the species naturally grows tucked beneath shrubs and rock overhangs and scorches in harsh direct sun. Water only once the soil has fully dried, and reduce watering further in winter, when growth slows. It offsets readily from the base, forming small clumps that can be divided and repotted once they crowd their container.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Pot offsets in a fast-draining succulent mix and grow in bright indirect light or light shade, protecting from direct hot midday sun.

directions: Gasteria brachyphylla is a compact, slow-growing species from the Western Cape of South Africa, forming tight rosettes of short, thick, blunt-tipped leaves in a distichous fan when young that becomes more spirally arranged with age. Grow in bright indirect light or dappled shade in a fast-draining, mineral-rich succulent mix, since it naturally grows sheltered under rock overhangs and low shrubs in its native habitat and can scorch in intense direct sun. Water sparingly, letting the soil dry completely between waterings, and cut back further during the winter rest period. It clusters slowly into small colonies that can be divided for propagation once offsets have their own roots.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Pot offsets in a fast-draining succulent mix and grow in bright indirect light or light shade, sheltering from harsh direct midday sun.

directions: Gasteria baylissiana is a small, clump-forming species restricted in the wild to rocky outcrops near Uitenhage in South Africa's Eastern Cape, where it grows wedged into crevices and beneath scrub in dappled shade. Its thick, dark green, tuberculate leaves form a compact rosette that stays low and dense even at maturity. Grow in a fast-draining, gritty succulent mix in bright indirect light or light shade, watering only once the soil has dried out fully and withholding most water in winter. It offsets steadily to form small clumping colonies that can be divided for propagation once individual rosettes have rooted.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix in full sun; allow cut ends to callus for several days before inserting into soil.

directions: Macrantha is a large-growing selection of pig's ear prized for its oversized, rounded, chalky gray-green leaves rimmed in red, noticeably bigger and bolder than the straight species. It develops into a substantial shrubby succulent on thick, woody stems, best grown in very well-drained, gritty soil in full sun to bring out the strongest red leaf margins. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing the soil to dry completely between waterings, and withhold water further in winter when growth slows. In late winter or spring, mature plants send up tall flower stalks bearing hanging clusters of orange-red bell-shaped blooms that attract hummingbirds. Propagate easily from stem or even single-leaf cuttings allowed to callus before rooting.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
